name: physical dimension as a type-level attribute
essential_semantics: A quantity carries a dimension (length, mass, time, ...) expressible as a vector of exponents over base dimensions, checked independently of the chosen unit.
canonical_example: velocity has dimension L T^-1
rationale: Dimensional analysis is a checkable soundness discipline over scientific mathematics; dimension is coarser and more robust than unit and must be tracked separately.

name: declared system of base dimensions
essential_semantics: The set of independent base dimensions is declared (SI's seven, or a domain-specific set) and extensible, rather than hard-coded.
canonical_example: SI base dimensions: L, M, T, I, Theta, N, J
rationale: Different fields use different base sets (e.g. adding currency or information); a fixed set silently excludes those domains.

name: unit of measurement
essential_semantics: A named scale for a dimension, where two units of the same dimension are convertible and units of different dimensions are not.
canonical_example: metre, foot and mile all have dimension L
rationale: Unit-mismatch failures are documented, expensive and entirely preventable by representation.

name: algebra of compound units
essential_semantics: Units multiply, divide and take rational powers, with a canonical form so that equivalent compound units compare equal.
canonical_example: N = kg m s^-2; J/s = W
rationale: Without canonicalisation of compound units, dimensionally equal quantities are wrongly reported as incompatible or vice versa.

name: quantity as value plus unit
essential_semantics: A single object pairing a magnitude with a unit, where the numeric magnitude alone is not the quantity.
rationale: Quantities compose with almost everything else in the ontology; if the unit is not attached to the value it will be lost at the first operation.

name: dimensional homogeneity checking
essential_semantics: Addition, subtraction, comparison and equality require matching dimensions; violation is rejected rather than coerced.
canonical_example: 1 m + 1 s is rejected
rationale: This is the primary payoff of unit tracking; a system that tracks units but does not enforce homogeneity gains nothing semantically.

name: conversion between commensurable units
essential_semantics: Exact or documented conversion factors between units of the same dimension, with the conversion recorded as a transformation rather than silently applied.
canonical_example: 1 inch = 25.4 mm exactly
rationale: Some conversions are exact and some are approximate; conflating them injects unrecorded error.

name: affine (offset) units and the difference/absolute distinction
essential_semantics: Units with a non-zero origin (Celsius, Fahrenheit, dates) where differences are ratio-scaled but absolutes are not, so multiplication by a scalar is invalid.
canonical_example: a 10 degC rise is 10 K, but 10 degC is 283.15 K
rationale: Doubling a temperature in Celsius is meaningless; this is the unit-level analogue of the point/vector distinction and is very commonly wrong.

name: metric prefixes and scale factors
essential_semantics: Prefixes as exact powers of ten (or two) composed with a base unit, not as separate units.
canonical_example: 1 km = 10^3 m exactly
rationale: Prefix handling determines whether km and m canonicalise together; getting it wrong produces spurious incompatibilities.

name: dimensionless quantities
essential_semantics: Quantities whose dimension vector is zero, which may still carry a unit-like tag (radian, percent, dB) that is semantically meaningful.
canonical_example: a strain of 0.002, an angle in radians
rationale: Dimensionless is not the same as unitless; radians and percent are dimensionless but not interchangeable.

name: dimensionless-argument requirement for transcendental functions
essential_semantics: exp, log, sin and similar require dimensionless arguments; a dimensionful argument must be rejected or explained.
canonical_example: log(x) with x in metres is ill-formed; log(x/x0) is not
rationale: It is a sharp, mechanically checkable rule that catches a whole class of modelling errors, notably in log-transformed regressions.

name: logarithmic scales and reference values
essential_semantics: Log-scaled quantities (dB, pH, magnitudes) are logs of ratios to a stated reference, and the reference is part of the quantity.
canonical_example: dB SPL is referenced to 20 micropascals
rationale: Reporting decibels without a reference is an incomplete quantity, a small but real semantic omission.

name: dimensionless groups and the Buckingham pi theorem
essential_semantics: Named combinations that are dimensionless by construction, with derivation from the dimension matrix.
canonical_example: Reynolds number Re = rho v L / mu
rationale: It shows dimensional analysis has real inferential content (a rank computation), not merely a checking role.

name: physical constants with units and provenance
essential_semantics: Named constants carrying a unit, an uncertainty and a defining source, with exact-by-definition constants distinguished from measured ones.
canonical_example: c = 299792458 m/s exactly; G is measured with uncertainty
rationale: The exact/measured distinction among constants directly affects error propagation.

name: measurement uncertainty attached to a quantity
essential_semantics: A value with a stated uncertainty and its interpretation (standard uncertainty, coverage interval), distinct from a probability distribution but relatable to one.
rationale: Uncertainty is a first-class attribute of measured data; dropping it converts a measurement into a false exact value.

name: propagation of uncertainty through operations
essential_semantics: Derived quantities carry uncertainties computed under stated assumptions (linearisation, independence of inputs).
canonical_example: for z = xy, relative uncertainties add in quadrature if x and y are independent
rationale: The independence assumption behind quadrature addition is usually unstated and often false.

name: precision of a reported value
essential_semantics: The number of meaningful digits is information about the value and is not increased by arithmetic.
canonical_example: 2.0 m is not the same claim as 2.000 m
rationale: Reporting more digits than justified is a common way computation manufactures false confidence.

name: units of a derivative
essential_semantics: d y / d x has the unit of y divided by the unit of x, computed automatically and correctly for higher orders.
canonical_example: d(position in m)/d(time in s) is m/s; the second derivative is m/s^2
rationale: A unit system that does not derive derivative units is not integrated with the calculus and will silently drop or corrupt units.

name: units of an integral
essential_semantics: The differential contributes its unit: integrating y d x yields units of y times units of x.
canonical_example: integral of power (W) dt (s) yields energy (J)
rationale: The measure carries units; this is also why a probability density has reciprocal units of its variate, a fact almost always lost.

name: random variables and distribution parameters with units
essential_semantics: A random variable may be dimensionful, in which case location and scale parameters share its unit, variance has squared units, and shape parameters must be dimensionless.
canonical_example: H ~ Normal(mu = 1.7 m, sigma = 0.1 m), Var(H) in m^2
rationale: The interaction of units with distribution parameter roles is a demanding cross-domain composition that almost no system handles fully.

name: reference frame of a physical quantity
essential_semantics: Vector quantities are expressed relative to a named frame, and combining quantities from different frames requires an explicit transformation.
canonical_example: velocity expressed in the body frame versus the inertial frame
rationale: Frame mismatch is the vector analogue of unit mismatch and causes equally serious errors in engineering.

name: units on vector, matrix and tensor components
essential_semantics: A unit may apply uniformly to a tensor or vary per component (as in a mixed-unit state vector), and this must be representable.
canonical_example: a state vector holding position in m and velocity in m/s
rationale: Mixed-unit vectors are common in control and state-space models and break naive per-array unit tagging.

name: counts, proportions and rates distinguished
essential_semantics: A dimensionless count, a proportion in [0,1] and a rate per unit of something are different quantity kinds despite all being numbers.
canonical_example: 17 events, 0.34 proportion, 2.1 events per hour
rationale: Poisson rates versus counts versus proportions are routinely mixed up in modelling, and the confusion is representable and preventable.

name: instants versus durations
essential_semantics: A time instant is a point on an affine timeline and a duration is a vector; only durations may be added or scaled.
canonical_example: t2 - t1 is a duration; t1 + t2 is meaningless
rationale: Time-series modelling constantly mixes instants and durations; it is the most frequently encountered affine-unit case.

name: conservation and balance relations
essential_semantics: A statement that a quantity's total is invariant or that inflow equals outflow, checkable dimensionally and structurally.
canonical_example: mass in equals mass out plus accumulation
rationale: Balance equations are a recurring scientific pattern whose dimensional consistency is a strong correctness signal.
